n: Alma, the chief missionary of the Nephite church, pours out a heartfelt wish: if only he were an angel, he could preach repentance to everyone on earth at once with a voice no one could ignore.

f.g: A trumpet, used in ancient Israel to call people together or announce something urgent.

n: His motive is love, not fame. He longs for every person to hear about repentance and God’s plan to redeem them, so that the sorrow sin causes would end everywhere.
Alma catches himself. Wishing for a different role than the one God gave him is a kind of discontent. True disciples serve faithfully where they have been placed.

f.g: Assigned or given as one’s portion.

n: God respects agency. He gives people what they truly desire—life or death, salvation or destruction—and those outcomes follow fixed, fair laws. Alma should not try to stir up or overturn that just arrangement.

f.g: To rake up or disturb, like a harrow breaking up soil.

n: Everyone eventually meets both good and evil. Those who cannot tell the difference (like little children) are not held guilty, but those who know are judged by what they choose and desire.
Knowing that God handles things justly, Alma asks himself why he should want anything more than to do the work he was actually called to do.
He repeats the question to settle it in his own heart: there is no need to wish for an angel’s trumpet voice.
God is not neglecting the rest of the world. He raises up teachers among every nation, in their own language, giving each people as much truth as He wisely sees they are ready for.

f.w: of their own nation and tongue

n: Alma finds his glory not in himself but in his calling. His greatest joy is the hope of being God’s instrument to help even one person repent.

f.w: instrument in the hands of God

n: Seeing others truly turn to the Lord fills Alma with joy and reminds him of his own conversion, when God heard his prayer and reached out to rescue him.

f.g: Sorry for sin and ready to change.

n: Alma also remembers his ancestors’ captivity and how the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob delivered them. Remembering past deliverance builds faith for the present.
The same God who freed Israel from Egypt also freed Alma’s own fathers (the people of Alma the Elder) from bondage. Alma sees one consistent, delivering God across history.
That God established His church, called Alma to preach, and blessed his work with success. Alma says this fills his joy completely.
His joy grows even fuller because of his friends, the sons of Mosiah, who spent fourteen years preaching among the Lamanites in the land of Nephi.
Their labor was intense, and thousands of Lamanites were converted. Alma rejoices at the great reward awaiting them.
Thinking of their success, Alma feels so much joy that it is almost as if his spirit could leave his body. It echoes Ammon’s overwhelming joy in Alma 27.
Alma closes with a prayer that his fellow missionaries and all their converts may dwell in God’s kingdom forever, never to leave, praising Him eternally.
